title: Clarity, Discipline and Consistency
hook: Why can't Neil tell if Southwest's 1971 low fare is a promise or just a price?
counterintuition: A visible choice is not credible just because it is tidy. It earns trust when Clarity of WHY gives Discipline of HOW a job before Consistency of WHAT asks the public to judge it.
tryThisNow: Watch one outgoing promise for 5 minutes during your first inbox scan; say the reason in one plain sentence, then write the visible act you saw.
keyTakeaway: A WHY earns trust when each visible choice owes it conduct. Southwest Airlines, Herb Kelleher, and Apple Inc. (Cupertino) show the same discipline: reason first, HOW owed, WHAT seen.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why can't Neil tell, on a family video call, whether Southwest's 1971 low fare is a promise or just a price? Southwest Airlines (the airline that began service in 1971 from Dallas and became a low-fare carrier) gives him the scene he needs. The fare is not the belief. It is the last visible sign of it.

Order does the work. Clarity of WHY names the reason; Discipline of HOW names the conduct; Consistency of WHAT lets outsiders see the same fit more than once. Put the fare first, and it has to explain too much. Put the reason first, and the fare can be judged against behavior. The fare did not make the belief; the belief made the fare readable.
breakdown.deepRead:
Alignment discipline works because the reason gives each action a job. If the action comes first, you can make it look neat, but it still cannot explain why anyone should trust it. Sequence matters.

On the call, Neil tries the easy line: low fares show Southwest's purpose. His family hears price talk. Then he puts Southwest Airlines back into behavior: the 1971 Dallas low-fare carrier had to make low fare visible in choices before the public could treat the offer as more than a sale.

Herb Kelleher (a Southwest Airlines cofounder) makes the conduct side harder to miss. The 1971 airline identity was reinforced through choices, humor, and hiring. Those details do not ask you to admire a person. They ask a plain question: What would a stranger see before the promise spoke?

Apple design consistency changes the setting. Apple Inc. (Cupertino) links the 1998 iMac and 2001 iPod through a clear challenger-and-design stance. It is not one product doing all the work. The fit repeats.

That is the strange part. You do not make a claim more trustworthy by adding a better-looking action at the end. You make the action easier to judge by letting the WHY set the debt first, then asking whether the HOW paid it.
breakdown.fullRead:
No title is required here. Before you send a promise, say the reason in one line and ask what act would let the other person see it. Put the reason before the visible act. That small pause keeps a neat tactic from pretending to be a belief.

Neil's call helps because it starts where a reader often starts: a visible offer that seems to speak for itself. It does not. A low fare may show a belief, or it may only show a low fare. Southwest Airlines gives the claim a visible setting because the 1971 Dallas low-fare carrier links the promise to behavior the public could inspect.

Herb Kelleher adds contrast, not more color. Cofounder is a role, not a year or a place. With Kelleher, the conduct runs through choices, humor, and hiring. If those actions fit the airline identity, the idea is less likely to be a one-off tale about a cheap seat. If they do not fit, the warm story fails.

Apple design consistency keeps the idea from getting too wide. Apple Inc. (Cupertino) links the 1998 iMac and 2001 iPod with a design stance a buyer could recognize. That does not mean every strong product from every organization proves the same point. The 1998 iMac is useful partly because it marks an edge.

Dallas does one narrow job. It grounds Southwest Airlines, which began service there in 1971. It does not help an Apple paragraph, even though the word feels concrete. A true fact attached to the wrong example makes the claim feel steadier than it is.

This is why clean purpose language is not enough. A sentence can sound calm and still leave no one wiser about what should change. You need a people-level debt: Neil owes Nancy a fare choice by Friday; Holly owes Preston the product cut before the launch note. When someone owes a visible act, the claim has a place to stand.

The same move works on small promises. A support reply, a hiring note, and a product choice can all drift when the visible thing arrives before the reason has named its job. Ask the plain diagnostic question: what must this person do so another person can see the same belief?

Do not wait for authority. If you answer support notes, draft a hiring line, or choose one product feature, the same question fits: what conduct will make the claim visible to the person who has to trust it?

Use this with care. It does not rescue a false WHY, and it does not turn thin facts into strong evidence. When the setting changes, ask for fresh conduct. When you are still learning, treat the visible act as a probe. When no act appears, say less.

examples.title: 1971 Finds The Extra

planSpec.stakes: a claim that customers cannot see
planSpec.requiredBeat: spot the early signal before the miss spreads

examples.scenario: Suppose a project lead, Neil, is pricing a cheaper service tier. The early signal is 1971. He likes the Southwest Airlines note, but his tier still includes custom favors that would push the price up. The miss is almost public when he traces the year back to the airline that began service from Dallas as a low-fare carrier. He cuts the favors; the offer now shows the reason before it asks for trust.
examples.whatToDo: Skip this and the year turns into color. Say the WHY first: low fare has to be visible. Then remove the feature that makes the promise behave the other way.
examples.whyItMatters: Treat 1971 as background and you miss the cause. The Southwest Airlines fact matters because it lets a reader inspect behavior instead of swallowing a slogan.

examples.title: Humor Has A Debt

planSpec.stakes: a person story that does not change behavior
planSpec.requiredBeat: state the standard and name what remains broken

examples.scenario: At a hypothetical hiring calibration, training director Nancy states the standard: Herb Kelleher's humor only matters if it reinforces Southwest Airlines' 1971 identity through choices and hiring. A blue badge lies between her and Neil. "So charm wins?" he asks. "No. Fit wins." The new question helps, but the score still rewards charm without conduct.
examples.whatToDo: Let this slide and the cofounder story turns soft. Ask what humor owed low fare. Answer with choices that fit the identity, not charm by itself.
examples.whyItMatters: Miss the unpaid part and hiring half-changes. The interview has better words, but the score still accepts the wrong signal.

examples.title: The Add-On Leaves

planSpec.stakes: a clever feature that splits the signal
planSpec.requiredBeat: cut the attractive extra after the standard is already set

examples.scenario: Product lead Holly is already cutting the popular add-on. The standard came from design consistency at Apple Inc. (Cupertino): the 1998 iMac and 2001 iPod point in the same challenger and design direction, so one clever extra cannot split the signal. The demo loses its flash; the offer leaves easier to read.
examples.whatToDo: Avoid the cut and novelty wins. Remove the extra that makes the product choice point away from the reason.
examples.whyItMatters: Leave it in and the signal splits. Consistency costs the attractive add-on.

examples.title: Dallas Goes Home

planSpec.stakes: a true fact doing false work
planSpec.requiredBeat: catch the misplaced detail at the return moment

examples.scenario: At a hypothetical draft handoff, Neil spots the miss as the reply-all email waits to send: Dallas is sitting under the product-design section. Southwest Airlines began service from Dallas in 1971, so the city cannot ground that paragraph. He stops the note, moves Dallas back to the airline case, and the client gets a narrower claim.
examples.whatToDo: Leave it alone and a true fact misleads. Stop the send. Put Dallas with Southwest. Write the Apple line without borrowed grounding.
examples.whyItMatters: Let Dallas sit there and the reader trusts the wrong link. Tie each hard fact to the example that actually carries it.

examples.title: The Update Waits

planSpec.requiredBeat: trace the miss after the talk and set the return point

examples.scenario: After a hypothetical staff update falls flat, strategist Preston traces the miss from the last sentence. A birthday-card envelope sits beside his laptop. The talk used purpose words, but none tied to Southwest Airlines' 1971 low-fare carrier setting, Herb Kelleher's cofounder role, or Apple Inc. (Cupertino) around the 1998 iMac. He pauses the wider claim; the owed behavior is still due.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the trace and purpose words do all the lifting. Shrink the claim to one named anchor, then wait until behavior can bear it.
examples.whyItMatters: Leave the gap and people cannot inspect anything. The pause has value because it keeps clean words from outrunning conduct.

questions.prompt: A product team already uses Southwest and Kelleher, but needs a source-backed technology setting. What should come next?
choices: Use Apple design consistency in Cupertino to press a nearby misconception from a new setting.
Keep every example inside Southwest so the last section repeats the strongest airline pattern.
Add a broad technology label so the reader feels the lesson has reached modern products.
questions.explanation: Apple design consistency supplies the source-backed change in setting. Staying inside Southwest is tempting, but it restamps the same sentence instead of probing a nearby error.

questions.prompt: The Kelleher section failed because it sounded like the Southwest section with another name. Which earlier choice caused that?
choices: The writer made 1971 too narrow, so the same year should have covered both airline units.
The writer flattened cofounder into a generic business stamp, so Kelleher lost his separate contrast.
The writer waited too long to add Apple, so the person example had no later product support.
questions.explanation: Cofounder is the factual token Kelleher adds. The 1971 answer sounds orderly, but it asks the same stamp to do contrast work it cannot do.

questions.prompt: A staff memo sounds purposeful, but it could fit almost any organization. What is actually missing?
choices: It reaches too many readers, so the claim should be saved for a smaller internal group.
It names too many concrete examples, so the lesson should rise above airlines, products, and named roles.
It lacks separate hard specifics from Southwest Airlines, Herb Kelleher, and Apple design consistency.
questions.explanation: Generic purpose language needs named anchors. The rise-above-examples choice is appealing, but it removes the concrete material the memo is missing.

questions.prompt: A team treats the 1998 iMac as permission to apply the idea to every organization it likes. What follows?
choices: The claim gets stronger because a known product makes each added organization easier to trust.
The claim only needs a later product because more examples would make the wider reach fair.
The limit disappears, and the idea moves into settings the source facts did not earn.
questions.explanation: The 1998 iMac marks where the idea stops. A later-product answer still overreaches unless the new setting brings conduct of its own.

questions.prompt: During rollout, Clarity, Discipline and Consistency became one catchy word; later no one knew what to fix. What failed earlier?
choices: They blended the jobs, so reason, conduct, and visible WHAT could not be diagnosed.
They shortened the phrase too late, so people had already learned the longer wording first.
They kept the airline example too small, so product decisions could not use the same lesson.
questions.explanation: The local frame gives each member a job. The timing answer treats wording as the issue, but the real failure is that distinct functions got merged.

questions.prompt: Neil says Southwest alone proves alignment discipline. What should Nancy do before the lesson gets broader?
choices: Bring in Herb Kelleher as a second anchor so the pattern has to survive comparison.
Stay inside Southwest Airlines and make Dallas carry more weight before any person enters.
Jump straight to Apple design consistency because products are easier to see than conduct.
questions.explanation: Kelleher makes comparison possible. Loading more onto Dallas stays inside Southwest, so it cannot show whether the pattern survives a second anchor.

questions.prompt: A launch starts with a neat HOW, then adds WHY after people react. What should be diagnosed first?
choices: The HOW reached the wrong audience, so the offer should aim at a different group before launch.
The sequence is reversed; the tactic is carrying the premise that should have framed it.
The WHY arrived too early to use response, so the team should wait for later reaction.
questions.explanation: Clarity of WHY has to frame Discipline of HOW. The audience choice changes the target, but the defect is order: the tactic is carrying the premise.

questions.prompt: After the client note failed, Dallas was found inside an Apple design section because it sounded concrete. What caused the failure?
choices: Dallas was used too briefly, so the detail needed to appear in more sections before Apple design carried it.
The sentence arrived too late, so an earlier mention would have made the true place easier to trust.
Dallas was attached to the wrong example, turning a true Southwest Airlines detail into false support.
questions.explanation: Dallas belongs with Southwest Airlines. The earlier-mention choice changes timing, but the failure is attachment: the real detail supports the wrong example.

questions.prompt: Which move best serves the reader when Neil wants one quick Southwest mention before broad purpose advice?
choices: Use Southwest Airlines as a warm opening, then let broad advice carry the claim once the reader is oriented.
Tie Southwest Airlines and 1971 to visible conduct, so the reader can judge more than the slogan.
Save 1971 for the last paragraph, after the airline name has built enough trust to carry the advice.
questions.explanation: Southwest Airlines is evidence, not scenery. The warm-opening choice leaves the advice floating, while the key links 1971 to conduct a reader can inspect.

reviewCards.front: What order keeps a tactic from doing too much?
reviewCards.back: Name the WHY before the HOW. If conduct comes first, the tactic has to explain a reason it did not create.

reviewCards.front: How do the three parts split the job?
reviewCards.back: Clarity of WHY states the reason, Discipline of HOW names the conduct, and Consistency of WHAT gives other people something visible to inspect. Blend them and diagnosis turns soft.

reviewCards.front: Why is Southwest not just an opener?
reviewCards.back: Southwest Airlines gives the idea behavior to inspect: the 1971 Dallas low-fare setting makes the claim visible instead of decorative.

reviewCards.front: What does a second anchor add?
reviewCards.back: Herb Kelleher gives the comparison a different token: cofounder. A lone example may illustrate; a second anchor shows whether the pattern survives a change in who is acting.

reviewCards.front: How can a true detail mislead?
reviewCards.back: A true detail misleads when it is attached to a claim it cannot support. Dallas belongs with Southwest Airlines; elsewhere it can make a false link feel grounded.

reviewCards.front: When should a vivid product example narrow the claim?
reviewCards.back: Narrow the claim when a product detail only supports one setting. The 1998 iMac can show where the idea stops as well as where it works.

reviewCards.front: How do you keep purpose words from floating?
reviewCards.back: Tie the promise to separate hard specifics from Southwest Airlines, Herb Kelleher, and Apple design consistency. If no behavior, role, or product choice appears, say less.

implementationPlan.title: Make The Act Owed
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use a promise as a debt, not a decoration. Say the WHY, name the HOW someone owes, and decide what visible WHAT another person could see. If you cannot name the act, shrink the promise until you can.

ifThenPlans.context: One outgoing message promises a benefit.
ifThenPlans.plan: If one outgoing message promises a benefit, then say the WHY and count 1 visible WHAT the recipient could see by end of day.

ifThenPlans.context: A tactic feels neat before the reason is clear.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a HOW feels neat before the WHY is clear, then count 1 reason it must serve before you keep it.
If Dallas sounds useful outside Southwest Airlines, then count 1 source it belongs to before you use it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Bolt this onto tomorrow's coffee routine: before the first sip, say the reason behind 1 promise you will make today and 1 act that would let someone see it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Every Friday before shutdown, say aloud: "The WHY was __. The HOW owed was __. The visible WHAT was __." If a blank stays blank, make the coming week's promise smaller.

memorableLines.text: What would a stranger see before the promise spoke?
memorableLines.why: It ties Southwest Airlines and 1971 to behavior a stranger can inspect.

memorableLines.text: Put the reason before the visible act.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the Dallas and Southwest Airlines discipline into a short command.

memorableLines.text: The fare did not make the belief; the belief made the fare readable.
memorableLines.why: It reverses the default reading of Southwest Airlines' 1971 low fare and points back to WHY before HOW.
